A long-sleeved V-neck cotton T-shirt, a real plain T-shirt and not a real garment, covered edge to edge in a bold flat-colour illustration with thick black outlines, designed to make the shirt look like the outfit of a bog witch. No plain shirt fabric shows except the ribbed collar band, because the outfit fills the whole shirt. The outfit is printed across the whole front, over the shoulders and down both sleeves, showing a muddy cloak with reeds. Turn the shirt around and the back carries the matching back of the outfit, printed edge to edge with nothing left plain. One continuous print of the outfit's cloth covers the shirt from collar band to hem and out to both sleeve hems. The shirt keeps the outline of an ordinary T-shirt, round neckline, straight side seams, sleeves, and a straight open hem. Only the upper garment is printed, running all the way down to the shirt's straight hem. The outfit's collar meets the real collar band, its shoulders sit on the real shoulder seams and its sleeves fill the real sleeves, all in one piece of printed cloth. The uniform fills the whole straight-sided shirt shape edge to edge, the same width at chest, waist and hem. The shirt is a long-sleeved T-shirt matching the outfit's long sleeves, printed with the sleeves and cuffs all the way down to the wrist hems. The sleeve hems are cut at an angle, slanted, pointed or curved, to follow the outfit's own cuffs, and the print follows that edge exactly. All textures, transparencies and sheens are printed patterns on solid cotton. Only the outfit's fabric, trims and fastenings are pictured, spread across the entire shirt as a continuous pattern. The illusion is purely flat and two-dimensional, with no real fabric, buttons or pockets beyond the print. It carries enough of the costume to be unmistakable, its pockets, flaps and trims, the most recognisable props and accessories of the outfit as appliqué pieces and the lower garment's colours and pattern as a band across the hem, all in the outfit's own colours.

To show the wrist on the wearer's forearms, the shirt is made with sleeves that run all the way to the wrist, and the printed wrist appear on those lengthened sleeves. It is a flat print, not a framed picture, not a small centred graphic, not a standing figure and not a drawing of a garment on a hanger. The tee is clearly a costume tee, not a plain shirt, it shows the held item or gear of the outfit, shown as a patch or large motif on the chest or a sleeve, the most recognisable props and accessories of the outfit as appliqué pieces and the headwear's emblem or crest worked into the chest, so anyone can tell at a glance what outfit it stands for.

The printed outfit runs from the neckline to the hem and from one sleeve hem to the other, its shoulders on the shirt's shoulder seams, showing a golden armoured robe. Front and back are both fully printed, the back showing how the same outfit looks from behind. One continuous print of the outfit's cloth covers the shirt from collar band to hem and out to both sleeve hems. The shirt is a standard T-shirt shape with a straight hem across the bottom. The shirt is an ordinary T-shirt ending in a straight bottom hem, and the garment printed on it runs straight down the whole shirt to that hem. The outfit's collar meets the real collar band, its shoulders sit on the real shoulder seams and its sleeves fill the real sleeves, all in one piece of printed cloth. The outfit is laid out on the shirt's own rectangle shape, fully covering it from side seam to side seam. The shirt is a long-sleeved T-shirt matching the outfit's long sleeves, printed with the sleeves and cuffs all the way down to the wrist hems. All textures, transparencies and sheens are printed patterns on solid cotton. Only the outfit's fabric, trims and fastenings are pictured, spread across the entire shirt as a continuous pattern. It also shows a printed collar around the real neckline and printed gloves emerging at the sleeve hems. Tiny printed shadows and fold lines suggest the garment without any real depth. To read as a costume rather than a plain top, it adds the collar, neckwear and fastenings of the outfit, the lower garment's colours and pattern as a band across the hem and its pockets, flaps and trims, bold and large enough to identify the outfit from across a room.

The printed outfit runs from the neckline to the hem and from one sleeve hem to the other, its shoulders on the shirt's shoulder seams, showing a huge ball gown with a tiara. Front and back are both fully printed, the back showing how the same outfit looks from behind. The outfit's own cloth covers the whole shirt as one continuous print, so shoulders, sleeves and body are all in the outfit's colours. It is an ordinary T-shirt in shape, with a straight open hem and sleeves cut to match the outfit's sleeves. The printed top garment continues down the shirt to its straight hem, with at most a belt or sash at the waist. The outfit's collar meets the real collar band, its shoulders sit on the real shoulder seams and its sleeves fill the real sleeves, all in one piece of printed cloth. The outfit is laid out on the shirt's own rectangle shape, fully covering it from side seam to side seam. The shirt is a long-sleeved T-shirt matching the outfit's long sleeves, printed with the sleeves and cuffs all the way down to the wrist hems. The shirt is solid opaque cotton and every texture and sheen is a printed picture. Only the outfit's fabric, trims and fastenings are pictured, spread across the entire shirt as a continuous pattern. It also shows printed cuffs and wrists at the sleeve hems. It is the kind of novelty tee that tricks the eye from across a room. The tee is clearly a costume tee, not a plain shirt, it shows the lower garment's colours and pattern as a band across the hem, the held item or gear of the outfit, shown as a patch or large motif on the chest or a sleeve and the outfit's patches, insignia and emblems, so anyone can tell at a glance what outfit it stands for.
A long-sleeved V-neck cotton T-shirt, a real plain T-shirt and not a real garment, covered edge to edge in a hand-drawn line-art print with flat colour fills, designed to make the shirt look like the outfit of a black knight. No plain shirt fabric shows except the ribbed collar band, because the outfit fills the whole shirt. The shirt's neckline is the outfit's collar opening, the shirt's sleeves carry the outfit's sleeves, and the shirt's hem is the outfit's lower edge, showing blackened plate armour with a tattered cape. Front and back are both fully printed, the back showing how the same outfit looks from behind. The outfit's fabric runs seamlessly over the shoulders and down the sleeves, every part of the shirt in the outfit's own colours and textures. The shirt is a standard T-shirt shape with a straight hem across the bottom. The shirt is an ordinary T-shirt ending in a straight bottom hem, and the garment printed on it runs straight down the whole shirt to that hem. The print is cut exactly to the shirt, neck, shoulders, armholes, sleeves and hem are all covered in the outfit's own fabric. The uniform fills the whole straight-sided shirt shape edge to edge, the same width at chest, waist and hem. A long-sleeved shirt is used so the outfit's long sleeves fit exactly, printed full length to the shirt's wrist hems. The sleeve hems are cut at an angle, slanted, pointed or curved, to follow the outfit's own cuffs, and the print follows that edge exactly. The shirt is solid opaque cotton and every texture and sheen is a printed picture. The picture is only the garment, its cloth, seams, buttons and trims laid flat across the whole shirt like a sewing pattern. It is a trompe-l'oeil T-shirt, a plain cotton shirt pretending to be the outfit. To read as a costume rather than a plain top, it adds the lower garment's colours and pattern as a band across the hem, the collar, neckwear and fastenings of the outfit and the footwear's trim colours as stripes on the cuffs and hem, bold and large enough to identify the outfit from across a room.

The printed outfit runs from the neckline to the hem and from one sleeve hem to the other, its shoulders on the shirt's shoulder seams, showing a patched leather cloak with a bandolier. The print wraps all the way round, the back of the shirt shows the rear of the outfit from the back collar to the hem and along both sleeves. One continuous print of the outfit's cloth covers the shirt from collar band to hem and out to both sleeve hems. The shirt is a standard T-shirt shape with a straight hem across the bottom. The printed top garment continues down the shirt to its straight hem, with at most a belt or sash at the waist. The print is cut exactly to the shirt, neck, shoulders, armholes, sleeves and hem are all covered in the outfit's own fabric. The uniform fills the whole straight-sided shirt shape edge to edge, the same width at chest, waist and hem. A long-sleeved shirt is used so the outfit's long sleeves fit exactly, printed full length to the shirt's wrist hems. The sleeve hems are cut at an angle, slanted, pointed or curved, to follow the outfit's own cuffs, and the print follows that edge exactly. The shirt is solid opaque cotton and every texture and sheen is a printed picture. The picture is only the garment, its cloth, seams, buttons and trims laid flat across the whole shirt like a sewing pattern. It is the kind of novelty tee that tricks the eye from across a room. To read as a costume rather than a plain top, it adds the collar, neckwear and fastenings of the outfit, the held item or gear of the outfit, shown as a patch or large motif on the chest or a sleeve and the lower garment's colours and pattern as a band across the hem, bold and large enough to identify the outfit from across a room.

The printed outfit runs from the neckline to the hem and from one sleeve hem to the other, its shoulders on the shirt's shoulder seams, showing a segmented metal armour suit with glowing vents. Turn the shirt around and the back carries the matching back of the outfit, printed edge to edge with nothing left plain. The outfit's fabric runs seamlessly over the shoulders and down the sleeves, every part of the shirt in the outfit's own colours and textures. It is an ordinary T-shirt in shape, with a straight open hem and sleeves cut to match the outfit's sleeves. The printed top garment continues down the shirt to its straight hem, with at most a belt or sash at the waist. The outfit's cloth runs unbroken from the collar band across both shoulders and down both sleeves to their hems, so every part of the shirt is outfit cloth. The outfit is laid out on the shirt's own rectangle shape, fully covering it from side seam to side seam. A long-sleeved shirt is used so the outfit's long sleeves fit exactly, printed full length to the shirt's wrist hems. The shirt is solid opaque cotton and every texture and sheen is a printed picture. The picture is only the garment, its cloth, seams, buttons and trims laid flat across the whole shirt like a sewing pattern. It may also show a flat printed line of cleavage in __clothing_uniform_tee_skin__ at a low or sweetheart neckline, all as flat ink. It also shows printed cuffs and wrists at the sleeve hems. Tiny printed shadows and fold lines suggest the garment without any real depth. To read as a costume rather than a plain top, it adds the footwear's trim colours as stripes on the cuffs and hem, the lower garment's colours and pattern as a band across the hem and the outfit's patches, insignia and emblems, bold and large enough to identify the outfit from across a room.

Every panel of the shirt, front, shoulders and sleeves, is a panel of the outfit, showing a leather jacket over a loose shirt. Front and back are both fully printed, the back showing how the same outfit looks from behind. The outfit's fabric runs seamlessly over the shoulders and down the sleeves, every part of the shirt in the outfit's own colours and textures. The shirt is a standard T-shirt shape with a straight hem across the bottom. The shirt is an ordinary T-shirt ending in a straight bottom hem, and the garment printed on it runs straight down the whole shirt to that hem. The print is cut exactly to the shirt, neck, shoulders, armholes, sleeves and hem are all covered in the outfit's own fabric. The outfit is stretched to the shirt's own straight-sided shape and fills it completely, so it suits any body size. The shirt is a long-sleeved T-shirt matching the outfit's long sleeves, printed with the sleeves and cuffs all the way down to the wrist hems. The shirt is solid opaque cotton and every texture and sheen is a printed picture. Only the outfit's fabric, trims and fastenings are pictured, spread across the entire shirt as a continuous pattern. It may also show flat printed chest hair on __clothing_uniform_tee_skin__ showing at the open collar, all as flat ink. It also shows printed cuffs at the sleeve hems. The printed collar and lapels line up with the shirt's actual neckline. It carries enough of the costume to be unmistakable, the held item or gear of the outfit, shown as a patch or large motif on the chest or a sleeve, the most recognisable props and accessories of the outfit as appliqué pieces and its pockets, flaps and trims, all in the outfit's own colours.

Every panel of the shirt, front, shoulders and sleeves, is a panel of the outfit, showing a padded suit with armour pads. Turn the shirt around and the back carries the matching back of the outfit, printed edge to edge with nothing left plain. The outfit's fabric runs seamlessly over the shoulders and down the sleeves, every part of the shirt in the outfit's own colours and textures. It is an ordinary T-shirt in shape, with a straight open hem and sleeves cut to match the outfit's sleeves. Only the upper garment is printed, running all the way down to the shirt's straight hem. The outfit's collar meets the real collar band, its shoulders sit on the real shoulder seams and its sleeves fill the real sleeves, all in one piece of printed cloth. The uniform fills the whole straight-sided shirt shape edge to edge, the same width at chest, waist and hem. The shirt is a long-sleeved T-shirt matching the outfit's long sleeves, printed with the sleeves and cuffs all the way down to the wrist hems. All textures, transparencies and sheens are printed patterns on solid cotton. The picture is only the garment, its cloth, seams, buttons and trims laid flat across the whole shirt like a sewing pattern. It also shows printed cuffs where the sleeves end. The illusion is purely flat and two-dimensional, with no real fabric, buttons or pockets beyond the print. To read as a costume rather than a plain top, it adds the outfit's patches, insignia and emblems, the most recognisable props and accessories of the outfit as appliqué pieces and the collar, neckwear and fastenings of the outfit, bold and large enough to identify the outfit from across a room.

The outfit is printed across the whole front, over the shoulders and down both sleeves, showing a brocade coat with a half mask. Turn the shirt around and the back carries the matching back of the outfit, printed edge to edge with nothing left plain. The outfit's fabric runs seamlessly over the shoulders and down the sleeves, every part of the shirt in the outfit's own colours and textures. The shirt is a standard T-shirt shape with a straight hem across the bottom. Only the upper garment is printed, running all the way down to the shirt's straight hem. The outfit's collar meets the real collar band, its shoulders sit on the real shoulder seams and its sleeves fill the real sleeves, all in one piece of printed cloth. The uniform fills the whole straight-sided shirt shape edge to edge, the same width at chest, waist and hem. The shirt is a long-sleeved T-shirt matching the outfit's long sleeves, printed with the sleeves and cuffs all the way down to the wrist hems. All textures, transparencies and sheens are printed patterns on solid cotton. The print is the garment itself, flat and unfolded over the shirt, in its own cloth and colours. It also shows a printed collar continuing the outfit up to the neckline. It is a flat print, not a framed picture, not a small centred graphic, not a standing figure and not a drawing of a garment on a hanger. The tee is clearly a costume tee, not a plain shirt, it shows the belt, straps and buckles of the outfit, the collar, neckwear and fastenings of the outfit and its pockets, flaps and trims, so anyone can tell at a glance what outfit it stands for.

The printed outfit runs from the neckline to the hem and from one sleeve hem to the other, its shoulders on the shirt's shoulder seams, showing a leopard-print leotard. The print wraps all the way round, the back of the shirt shows the rear of the outfit from the back collar to the hem and along both sleeves. The outfit's fabric runs seamlessly over the shoulders and down the sleeves, every part of the shirt in the outfit's own colours and textures. It is an ordinary T-shirt in shape, with a straight open hem and sleeves cut to match the outfit's sleeves. The printed top garment continues down the shirt to its straight hem, with at most a belt or sash at the waist. The outfit's collar meets the real collar band, its shoulders sit on the real shoulder seams and its sleeves fill the real sleeves, all in one piece of printed cloth. The uniform fills the whole straight-sided shirt shape edge to edge, the same width at chest, waist and hem. The shirt is a short-sleeved T-shirt, and the outfit's sleeves are printed as short sleeves ending exactly at the shirt's sleeve hems. All textures, transparencies and sheens are printed patterns on solid cotton. The picture is only the garment, its cloth, seams, buttons and trims laid flat across the whole shirt like a sewing pattern. It also shows printed cuffs where the sleeves end. It is a flat print, not a framed picture, not a small centred graphic, not a standing figure and not a drawing of a garment on a hanger. It carries enough of the costume to be unmistakable, the headwear's emblem or crest worked into the chest, the most recognisable props and accessories of the outfit as appliqué pieces and the lower garment's colours and pattern as a band across the hem, all in the outfit's own colours.

Every panel of the shirt, front, shoulders and sleeves, is a panel of the outfit, showing a white kimono top with a long scarf. Front and back are both fully printed, the back showing how the same outfit looks from behind. The outfit's fabric runs seamlessly over the shoulders and down the sleeves, every part of the shirt in the outfit's own colours and textures. It is an ordinary T-shirt in shape, with a straight open hem and sleeves cut to match the outfit's sleeves. Only the upper garment is printed, running all the way down to the shirt's straight hem. The print is cut exactly to the shirt, neck, shoulders, armholes, sleeves and hem are all covered in the outfit's own fabric. The outfit is laid out on the shirt's own rectangle shape, fully covering it from side seam to side seam. The shirt's sleeves are tailored to end about two-thirds of the way down the arm, exactly where the outfit's sleeves end. The sleeve hems are cut at an angle, slanted, pointed or curved, to follow the outfit's own cuffs, and the print follows that edge exactly. The shirt is solid opaque cotton and every texture and sheen is a printed picture. Only the outfit's fabric, trims and fastenings are pictured, spread across the entire shirt as a continuous pattern. It also shows printed cuffs at the sleeve hems. It is a trompe-l'oeil T-shirt, a plain cotton shirt pretending to be the outfit. The tee is clearly a costume tee, not a plain shirt, it shows the belt, straps and buckles of the outfit, the outfit's patches, insignia and emblems and the held item or gear of the outfit, shown as a patch or large motif on the chest or a sleeve, so anyone can tell at a glance what outfit it stands for.
A three-quarter-sleeved scoop-neck cotton T-shirt, a real plain T-shirt and not a real garment, covered edge to edge in a comic-style inked illustration print, designed to make the shirt look like the outfit of a patterned-haori swordsperson. The outfit's colours flood the entire front and both sleeves as one continuous print, and the back carries the matching back of the outfit. The shirt's neckline is the outfit's collar opening, the shirt's sleeves carry the outfit's sleeves, and the shirt's hem is the outfit's lower edge, showing a patterned haori over a plain kimono. Turn the shirt around and the back carries the matching back of the outfit, printed edge to edge with nothing left plain. The outfit's fabric runs seamlessly over the shoulders and down the sleeves, every part of the shirt in the outfit's own colours and textures. It is an ordinary T-shirt in shape, with a straight open hem and sleeves cut to match the outfit's sleeves. The shirt is an ordinary T-shirt ending in a straight bottom hem, and the garment printed on it runs straight down the whole shirt to that hem. The print is cut exactly to the shirt, neck, shoulders, armholes, sleeves and hem are all covered in the outfit's own fabric. The outfit is stretched to the shirt's own straight-sided shape and fills it completely, so it suits any body size. The shirt's sleeves are tailored to end about two-thirds of the way down the arm, exactly where the outfit's sleeves end. The sleeve hems are cut at an angle, slanted, pointed or curved, to follow the outfit's own cuffs, and the print follows that edge exactly. Everything is flat ink on opaque cotton, lace, tulle, fur, feathers, sequins, armour and metal appear as printed patterns. Only the outfit's fabric, trims and fastenings are pictured, spread across the entire shirt as a continuous pattern. It also shows printed cuffs where the sleeves end. It is the kind of novelty tee that tricks the eye from across a room. To read as a costume rather than a plain top, it adds the most recognisable props and accessories of the outfit as appliqué pieces, the footwear's trim colours as stripes on the cuffs and hem and the held item or gear of the outfit, shown as a patch or large motif on the chest or a sleeve, bold and large enough to identify the outfit from across a room.
